newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls vs mark after US trade deficit widens.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls vs mark after US trade deficit widens.

text.p: The dollar fell against European currencies Wednesday after a sharp widening of the U.S. trade deficit prompted worries that a strong U.S. currency was hurting exports.
But the dollar rose against the yen amid concerns about Japan's troubled banking sector.
"The trade issue is definitely a raw nerve and has given the dollar some vulnerability," said Talbott Young, a vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank in Richmond, Va.
The Commerce Department said the U.S. international trade deficit increased 10.1 percent to $11.34 billion in September, from $10.3 billion in August.
The data came a day after complaints by the National Association of Manufacturers that the strong dollar would hurt exports by making U.S. products more expensive overseas.
The growing trade gap prompted short-term speculation that U.S. businesses might pressure the Clinton administration to abandon its strong-dollar policy, traders said.
As a result, the dollar traded at 1.4965 marks late Wednesday, down from 1.5055 marks late Tuesday.

But the dollar recovered against the yen after Japanese news agencies reported on Wednesday that Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) is expected to order Hanwa Bank, a small regional bank, to suspend most of its business on Friday.
This would mark the first time after World War II that the Japanese government has ordered a bank to suspend operations, the report said.

"If there is a domino effect, then maybe the Japanese MOF will have to have accommodate with interest rates to help Japanese financial institutions," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank in New York.
Such an accommodation would push Japanese interest rates lower, making borrowing costs less expensive for banks. It would also make yen deposits less attractive to investors.
This outlook lifted the dollar to 111.55 yen in late trading from 111.65 yen late Tuesday.

While the U.S.-Japan trade deficit has been a key issue in the yen's rise against the dollar, dealers shrugged off news of a 0.3 percent drop in the bilateral trade gap in September, after large monthly declines this year.
Earlier this week, Japan's October trade surplus with the United States widened for the first time since February 1995.
Early last year trade frictions were at a peak and the Clinton administration seemed to tolerate the dollar's slide to record lows in April to encourage Japan to buy more U.S. products.
In other trade, the British pound reached a new four-year high at $1.6820 on Wednesday. It closed at $1.6810, up from $1.6755 late Tuesday.
The dollar fell to 1.2662 Swiss francs from 1.2715 Swiss and to Canadian $1.3396 from C$1.3419.
